blueprint.purpose: To persuade garden members to approve a signal booster and study table at the garden shed so students without home internet can do homework
blueprint.audience: Members of the Hollis Creek Community Garden, many of them retired growers who care about cost and the plots, voting at the November meeting
blueprint.claim: The garden can cheaply and responsibly help close the homework gap for ridge families by improving the shed's Wi-Fi and adding a study space
blueprint.theme: rural broadband and the homework gap

planned_flaws.flaw: Vague thesis that neither requires proof nor previews the proposal
Insulting tone toward the very readers being asked to vote
Cost stated without addressing members' budget concerns
Missing transition signaling an additional proposal
Missing transition from objection to response
Does not acknowledge older members who studied without internet

provenance.venue_alias: Hollis Creek Community Garden bulletin board

g-lw41.title: Homework at the Garden Fence
paragraphs: Every Thursday evening this fall, a few cars have been parked along the fence of the Hollis Creek Community Garden with their engines off and their dome lights on.
Inside them are kids from up on Marrow Ridge doing homework, because the weak Wi-Fi from the garden shed reaches the gravel lot and their houses get no signal at all.
Internet is important for students these days.
My name is Tessa Lindqvist, and I was one of those kids last spring.
Our teachers post every assignment online, and the county's math program will not even load on a phone showing one bar.
My neighbor's son, Caleb, failed a chemistry quiz because the practice set timed out four times on his mother's hotspot.
Obviously, anyone who doesn't get this is clueless about how school works now.
The garden committee could fix part of this problem cheaply.
A signal booster mounted on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, according to the hardware co-op in Pell.
A picnic table under the shed awning, with one outdoor outlet, would let students work somewhere other than a cold car.
The garden already stays open until dusk, so no new hours would be needed.
Some members worry that teenagers will trample the beds or leave trash behind.
Students using the table would agree to stay by the shed and to pick up before leaving each night.
I am asking every member to vote yes at the November 9 meeting.

items.stem: Many garden members are retirees who keep a close eye on the committee's small budget. The writer wants to revise sentence 9 to address this audience's concern about cost. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, which is honestly nothing compared to what a good education is worth.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Dismisses the members' budget worry instead of addressing it.

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, less than last summer's new hoses, and my family has offered to pay half.
options.label: correct
options.why: Puts the cost in terms members know and reduces the burden on the budget, directly answering their concern.

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof would cost about 140 dollars, and it would probably pay for itself many times over someday.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Makes a vague, unsupported financial claim that does not reassure budget-minded readers.

options.text: A signal booster on the shed roof, a model with two antennas and a weatherproof case, is sold at the hardware co-op in Pell.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Adds product details but drops the cost entirely, ignoring the audience's concern.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 5 that respects members who finished school without the internet while explaining why students today cannot do the same. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Today the assignments exist only online, and the school stopped handing out printed packets two years ago.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Explains the change but does not acknowledge members who studied without the internet.

options.text: Many of you did homework with a library book and a pencil, which shows that the old way was always better for kids.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Undercuts the writer's own argument instead of explaining why students now need internet.

options.text: Many of you probably think kids today are lazy and just want to sit on their phones at the garden fence.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Assumes the worst of readers rather than respecting them, and explains nothing.

options.text: Many of you did homework with a library book and a pencil, but today the assignments themselves exist only online.
options.label: correct
options.why: Honors members' experience and explains the change that makes their approach impossible now.

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 10 with a transition that signals a second, separate improvement following the one described in sentence 9. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: For instance,
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Presents the table as an example of the booster, which it is not.

options.text: In contrast,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals opposition, but the table complements the booster.

options.text: As a result,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Wrongly implies the booster causes the table to exist.

options.text: In addition,
options.label: correct
options.why: Signals that the table is a further improvement added to the booster.

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 13 with a transition that shows the sentence is a response to the worry raised in sentence 12. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Similarly to that concern,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals likeness, but sentence 13 answers rather than resembles the worry.

options.text: To address that concern,
options.label: correct
options.why: Directly marks sentence 13 as the answer to the members' worry.

options.text: Despite that small concern,
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Belittles the members' worry and suggests the writer will disregard it.

options.text: Because of that concern,
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Mentions the concern but frames the promise as merely caused by it, not as a reply.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 14 that ends the flyer by reminding garden members that the proposal fits values they already hold as growers. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: If the vote fails, students will keep failing quizzes like Caleb did, and the committee will have to explain why it let that happen.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Ends on a threat that blames the readers instead of appealing to their values.

options.text: The signal booster from the co-op in Pell can be installed in about an afternoon by any member who owns a sturdy ladder.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Gives a practical detail rather than a closing appeal to shared values.

options.text: High-speed internet is now a basic need across the country, and every rural community will have to deal with the gap sooner or later.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Moves away from this garden and its members' values to a general national claim.

options.text: This garden has always shared its extra seedlings and spare tools with neighbors, and a table and a stronger signal would just be one more thing we share.
options.label: correct
options.why: Ties the proposal to the members' existing habit of sharing, so the ending appeals to values they already hold.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that explains how Caleb's experience supports the claim that students need a reliable connection. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Chemistry is widely considered one of the hardest subjects in high school, especially for students who struggle with math.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Suggests the subject was the problem, which works against the point about the connection.

options.text: His mother has since switched to a different phone plan, though the hotspot still drops out when it rains on the ridge.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Mentions the connection again but does not explain how the example supports the claim.

options.text: He knew the material, but a weak signal kept him from practicing it, so the connection decided his grade more than his effort did.
options.label: correct
options.why: Explains how the anecdote shows that unreliable access, not ability, hurt his grade.

options.text: Caleb is a junior this year and hopes to study nursing at a college somewhere in the state after he graduates.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Adds background about Caleb that has nothing to do with the claim.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 11 so that it admits a limit of the proposal without dropping the point that the garden's schedule would not have to change. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The garden already stays open until dusk, so no new hours would be needed, though in November dusk comes early enough that students would still have to finish some work elsewhere.
options.label: correct
options.why: Keeps the claim about hours and honestly notes that early dusk limits how much the table can help.

options.text: The garden already stays open until dusk, which most members agree is the best time of day to water seedlings and check the tomato beds for pests.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Wanders into gardening chores and never qualifies the claim about students.

options.text: The garden already stays open until dusk, but the committee should probably add evening hours, staffed by volunteers, so students can stay as late as they want to.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Admits a limit but drops the point that no schedule change is needed, which hurts the low-cost case.

options.text: The garden already stays open until dusk, so no new hours would be needed, and the table would give students all the study time they could ever need.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Makes the claim even bigger instead of admitting a limit.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 3 with a sentence that ends the introduction by linking the scene in sentences 1 and 2 to a decision the garden members themselves can make. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Those parked cars show a need that our own garden, with one small vote, is in a position to meet.
options.label: correct
options.why: It points back to the parked cars and names the members' vote as the way to respond, which sets up the proposal.

options.text: Across the country, rural families face a growing gap between home internet access and the demands of school.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: It widens the focus to the whole country and says nothing about the garden or the members' decision.

options.text: Those parked cars are the saddest sight in Hollis Creek, and every one of us should feel ashamed of it.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: It blames the readers being asked to vote and does not mention any decision they can make.

options.text: The Wi-Fi in the garden shed was first installed years ago so that the committee could keep its records online.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It adds background about the shed instead of connecting the scene to the members' choice.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 13 that gives evidence that students can be trusted to keep the promises described in that sentence. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Over six weeks of Thursdays in the lot, the students have left no litter, and two of them helped stack the compost bins.
options.label: correct
options.why: It offers a concrete record of past behavior showing the students already keep the area clean, which supports trusting the promises.

options.text: Teenagers today are often more responsible than older adults give them credit for, and most of them mean well.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: It is a general claim with no evidence, so it cannot prove that these students will keep their promises.

options.text: A picnic table made of recycled plastic would hold up through the winter and would need very little upkeep.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: It is about the table lasting, not about whether students will behave responsibly.

options.text: Many students on Marrow Ridge also have chores at home, sports after school, and long bus rides to the high school.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: It says something about the students but nothing about staying by the shed or picking up trash.

items.stem: The writer wants to combine sentences 4 and 5 into one sentence that makes clear her own experience last spring is the reason she understands the problem with online assignments. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: I am Tessa Lindqvist, and because I was one of those kids last spring, I know that our teachers post every assignment online and that the county's math program will not load on a phone showing one bar.
options.label: correct
options.why: The word because shows that her experience is the source of what she knows, and the two facts are joined in parallel that-clauses.

options.text: I am Tessa Lindqvist, I was one of those kids last spring, our teachers post every assignment online, and the county's math program will not load on a phone showing one bar.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: It strings the clauses together in a list that reads as a run-on and does not show any cause.

options.text: Although I am Tessa Lindqvist and was one of those kids last spring, our teachers post every assignment online, and the county's math program will not load on a phone showing one bar.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Although sets up a contrast that makes no sense here; her experience does not conflict with the facts.

options.text: I am Tessa Lindqvist, one of those kids last spring, and our teachers, who post every assignment online, use a county math program that will not load on a phone showing one bar.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: It combines the sentences smoothly but never shows that her experience is why she knows these facts.

blueprint.purpose: To announce the library's annual Transfer Night and persuade adult readers, especially those returning to school, that community college transfer pathways offer a real second chance
blueprint.audience: Patrons of a small-town public library, including adults who left school early and parents of college-bound teenagers
blueprint.claim: Transfer pathways turn community college into a reliable route to a four-year degree, so readers considering a second start should come to Transfer Night
blueprint.theme: community college transfer pathways and the idea of a second chance

planned_flaws.flaw: Vague thesis that does not preview the post's argument or require proof
Comma splice joining two independent clauses
Wordy, vague, overly casual definition of transfer pathways
Abstract definition lacks a clarifying comparison for unfamiliar readers
Does not address readers who see community college as a lesser fallback
Flat, offhand conclusion that gives no invitation, details, or return to the second-chance idea

provenance.note: Fictional draft; all names, places and institutions invented.

g-lw42.title: Draft: Why Transfer Night Matters
paragraphs: Every spring, the second-floor meeting room at the Harlan Ferry Public Library fills with folding chairs, a dented coffee urn, and people who are not sure they belong there.
Community college is a good thing for a lot of people.
Our annual Transfer Night, held this year on Thursday, April 17, brings advisors from Calloway Valley Community College and two state universities to answer questions one at a time.
Last year I met a man named Arturo Pell, who had left high school at seventeen to work in his uncle's tire shop.
At forty-one, he had just finished an associate degree at Calloway Valley, and he was trying to figure out which of his credits would count toward the nursing program at Ridgeline State University.
An advisor spent twenty minutes with him going over a printed transfer agreement, the sheet listed every Calloway Valley course that Ridgeline would accept.
He left with a plan and a highlighted copy of that sheet folded into his jacket pocket.
Arturo's story is not unusual.
Many students start at community colleges because tuition is lower, because classes meet at night, or because they need time to rebuild confidence after a rough start somewhere else.
Transfer pathways are basically like a whole bunch of agreements and stuff that colleges make so that what you learn at one place gets counted at another place, which is really important.
Without them, a returning student can lose a semester or more retaking classes he or she has already passed.
Anyway, that is pretty much what the night is about.
Hope to see you there.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 9 that addresses parents of college-bound teenagers who believe community college is a lesser choice than starting at a university. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Universities are often prestigious places, and many parents understandably dream of seeing their children attend one.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Reinforces the parents' belief rather than answering it, undercutting the writer's claim.

options.text: Honestly, anyone who still looks down on community college in this day and age just has not been paying attention.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Insults the very readers the writer hopes to persuade, likely alienating rather than reassuring them.

options.text: Some returning adults also choose community college because it lets them keep a full-time job while they study.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Addresses adult learners, not the parents of teenagers named in the goal.

options.text: For your teenager, starting close to home can mean the same degree at the end, earned with smaller classes and far less debt.
options.label: correct
options.why: Speaks directly to parents and answers their concern by stressing the same final degree plus concrete advantages.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 2 into a thesis that makes a defensible claim and previews the post's movement from Arturo's experience to an explanation of transfer pathways. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: As one patron's story shows, clear transfer pathways can turn community college from a detour into a reliable second chance at a degree.
options.label: correct
options.why: Makes an arguable claim about transfer pathways and previews both the anecdote and the explanation that follow.

options.text: Calloway Valley Community College offers more than forty associate degree programs, including nursing, welding, and accounting.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: States an unverified fact rather than a claim, and previews nothing about the post's structure.

options.text: Last spring, one patron learned exactly which of his credits would transfer to a nursing program at a state university.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Summarizes the anecdote only; it is a fact, not a claim, and omits the explanation of pathways.

options.text: Education is one of the most important things in life, and everyone deserves the chance to learn at any age.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: A sweeping, nearly undebatable generality that never mentions transfer pathways or the anecdote.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 that uses an analogy to help readers unfamiliar with college paperwork understand what a transfer agreement guarantees. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: These agreements are usually signed by college presidents and reviewed by state education boards every few years.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Adds procedural detail about the word 'agreement' but no analogy and no clarification of the guarantee.

options.text: A transfer agreement works like an exchange rate posted in advance: students know before enrolling what their coursework will be worth later.
options.label: correct
options.why: The exchange-rate analogy clarifies the key guarantee, that course value is known ahead of time, which links to sentence 11.

options.text: Earning a degree is like running a marathon, since it takes years of endurance and patience to reach the finish line.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: An analogy about perseverance, not about what a transfer agreement guarantees.

options.text: According to many advisors, roughly eight out of ten transfer students say the agreements saved them money and time.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Offers an unsourced statistic instead of an analogy and does not explain what the agreement is.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 10 so that it defines transfer pathways clearly and concisely in a tone suited to a library's public blog. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Transfer pathways are important because they are among the most significant features of the modern education system.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Formal in tone but circular; it never defines what transfer pathways actually are.

options.text: Transfer pathways are formal agreements between colleges that guarantee credits earned at one school will count at another.
options.label: correct
options.why: Precise, concise, and appropriately professional; removes the filler and vague wording.

options.text: Transfer pathways are basically deals that colleges make so your stuff from one school counts at the other one.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Shorter but keeps casual, vague wording ('basically,' 'stuff') unsuited to the blog.

options.text: Transfer pathways, which are agreements, are agreements between colleges, and these agreements make credits count elsewhere.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Redundantly repeats 'agreements' and remains wordy and awkward.

items.stem:
In sentence 6 (reproduced below), the writer wants to correct the punctuation so the two independent clauses are joined correctly while keeping the sentence's meaning.

An advisor spent twenty minutes with him going over a printed transfer agreement, the sheet listed every Calloway Valley course that Ridgeline would accept.

Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: agreement, the sheet, it listed
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Still a comma splice and adds a redundant pronoun.

options.text: agreement, and so therefore the sheet listed
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Falsely presents the listing as a result of the meeting and piles on redundant connectives.

options.text: agreement; the sheet listed
options.label: correct
options.why: A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses, fixing the comma splice.

options.text: agreement, however the sheet listed
options.label: convention_error
options.why: 'However' cannot join clauses after a comma, and it signals a contrast the sentence does not express.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 11 that gives evidence for the specific claim that students without transfer agreements can lose time retaking courses they already passed. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Every college in the state, without exception, now accepts every course from every other college, so no student will ever repeat a class again.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: An unsupported overstatement that also contradicts sentence 11 instead of supporting it.

options.text: Before Calloway Valley signed its agreement with Ridgeline, one Harlan Ferry student told our staff she had repeated three passed courses, costing her a full extra semester.
options.label: correct
options.why: Gives a concrete case of passed courses being retaken and time being lost, which is exactly what sentence 11 claims.

options.text: The advisors who come to Transfer Night are patient and friendly, and several of them started their own degrees at a community college years ago.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Describes the event's advisors. It gives no evidence that missing agreements make students repeat courses.

options.text: Tuition at Calloway Valley costs much less per credit than at either state university, which lets many patrons save money for the later years of a degree.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Supports the point about low cost in sentence 9, not the claim about lost semesters without agreements.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that admits transfer agreements have limits while still arguing that readers should come to Transfer Night. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Because so many courses fall outside these agreements, most returning students would probably be better off skipping community college entirely.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Mentions a limit but ends up undercutting the post's argument instead of keeping it.

options.text: The library's meeting room was also recently repainted, and new chairs replaced several of the dented folding ones from earlier years.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Off-topic detail that qualifies nothing about transfer pathways.

options.text: Agreements like that one guarantee that every class a student takes will count toward any degree at any university the student chooses.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Overstates the claim even more instead of qualifying it.

options.text: Not every course or major is covered by such an agreement, which is exactly why a conversation with an advisor before enrolling is worth an evening.
options.label: correct
options.why: Admits a real limit, then uses that limit as a reason to attend, so the qualification still serves the post's claim.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentences 12 and 13 with a conclusion that returns to the idea of a second chance and gives readers the practical details they need to attend Transfer Night. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: If you have a folder of old transcripts in a drawer, bring it to the second-floor meeting room on Thursday, April 17; a plan like the one Arturo carried home may be waiting for you.
options.label: correct
options.why: Gives the date and place, invites readers directly, and brings back Arturo's plan as an image of a second chance.

options.text: Community colleges have grown in many towns over the years, and more of them now offer night classes and online courses for working adults.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Gives general background instead of a closing invitation; it has no event details and no return to the second-chance idea.

options.text: Transfer Night is a chance to start over, and everyone who has ever regretted leaving school should feel welcome to stop by sometime soon.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Mentions starting over but leaves out the date and place, and 'stop by sometime soon' is vague about a single scheduled event.

options.text: Readers should note that the coffee urn will be replaced this year, so refreshments in the meeting room will be noticeably better than before.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Picks up a minor detail from sentence 1 and ignores both the invitation and the argument.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that explains how Arturo's experience supports the post's claim that transfer pathways make community college a reliable route to a four-year degree. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Because the agreement spelled out which courses counted, his associate degree became the first half of a nursing degree instead of a pile of uncertain credits.
options.label: correct
options.why: Connects the agreement in the story directly to the claim that pathways turn community college credit into progress toward a four-year degree.

options.text: His uncle's tire shop, where he had worked for over two decades, was located only a few blocks from the library on Main Street.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Adds an invented detail that does nothing to link the evidence to the claim.

options.text: Nursing is one of the most demanding fields a student can enter, and many hospitals in the region are short of qualified staff.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Moves the focus to the nursing workforce instead of explaining what the anecdote shows about transfer pathways.

options.text: He told me afterward that the advisor had been friendly and patient, which made the long evening feel shorter than he expected.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Praises the advisor's manner rather than explaining why the transfer agreement made his path reliable.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 2 ("Community college is a good thing for a lot of people.") so it keeps the same basic idea but speaks to hesitant adult readers in a warm, respectful tone without exaggerating. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: For many of our neighbors, community college has been a practical and welcoming place to begin again.
options.label: correct
options.why: Keeps the idea, sounds warm and respectful, and makes no inflated claim.

options.text: Honestly, community college is totally awesome and you'd be crazy not to sign up right away.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Slangy and pushy, and it hints that hesitant readers are foolish.

options.text: Community college is the single greatest opportunity any adult could ever hope to receive.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Exaggerates, which goes against the 'without exaggerating' goal.

options.text: Even people who failed at school the first time can still manage community college.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Talks down to readers by calling them failures, which is not respectful.

blueprint.purpose: To report on findings from a school music-history project about how conductors lead without making sound
blueprint.claim: Conductors lead mainly through breath and gesture, signals the players learn to read
blueprint.genre: report on a school project draft
blueprint.theme: orchestral conductors and the problem of leadership without sound

planned_flaws.flaw: vague thesis
evidence with no commentary
overstated claim
informal tone
wordy, informal sentence
empty conclusion

provenance.venue_alias: Halvern Ridge High School music-history class

g-lw43.title: The Silent Player: Watching a Conductor at Work
paragraphs: Conductors are interesting and there are many things to say about them.
For our music-history project, I spent three Thursday rehearsals watching Maestra Ilse Okonkwo-Dahl lead the Corlett Valley Youth Orchestra.
She is the only person on the stage who makes no sound at all.
Before the first rehearsal, the principal cellist told me that the musicians follow the conductor's breath more closely than her baton.
At the second rehearsal, I watched Okonkwo-Dahl inhale sharply just before the opening chord of the overture the group was learning, and all forty players came in together.
Later, when she forgot to breathe before the same chord, the entrance was ragged.
Conductors always control everything that happens in a performance.
In the third rehearsal, Okonkwo-Dahl stopped the brass section four times in ten minutes.
Honestly, the brass guys got kind of bossed around, but she never raised her voice.
She just lowered her left hand slowly, and the trumpets got softer, which was a thing that happened each time she did the hand thing, and it was pretty awesome to see.
In the end, conductors are a big deal.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 11 with a conclusion that sums up what her observations showed about how a conductor leads without making sound. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Over three rehearsals, I learned that a conductor's breath and hands can carry an orchestra.
options.label: correct
options.why: Draws together the breath evidence (paragraph 2) and the hand gesture evidence (paragraph 3) as the way she leads silently.

options.text: The trumpets got softer each time Okonkwo-Dahl lowered her hand.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Repeats one detail and leaves out the breath findings.

options.text: In the end, I think everyone should go and watch a youth orchestra rehearse.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Makes a recommendation rather than summing up what the observations showed.

options.text: Conductors have existed for centuries and have changed music history.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Sweeping historical claim the report never discusses.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 1 into a thesis that makes a claim requiring proof and previews the two kinds of silent signals the report goes on to discuss. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Though she makes no sound, a conductor leads through her breath and her hands.
options.label: correct
options.why: Makes an arguable claim and previews breath (paragraph 2) and hands (paragraph 3).

options.text: A conductor is the person who stands in front of an orchestra with a baton.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Gives a definition that needs no proof and previews nothing.

options.text: Conductors are fascinating people, and I learned a great deal about them.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Still vague; it makes no specific claim and previews nothing.

options.text: Conductors lead through their breath, which players follow more than the baton.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Previews only breath and leaves out the hand gestures in paragraph 3.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 7 so it qualifies the overstated claim while still introducing the conductor's control over the players in paragraph 3. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Some say conductors control everything, and I agree with them on this point.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Brings in a vague outside view and keeps the absolute claim.

options.text: Conductors completely control every note that each player in the orchestra makes.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Makes the overstatement stronger instead of qualifying it.

options.text: A conductor cannot play a note, but she can shape much of how the players sound.
options.label: correct
options.why: Limits the claim ('much of') and acknowledges the limit, while setting up her control over the brass.

options.text: Conductors have almost no real influence over how a performance sounds.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Swings to the opposite extreme and contradicts sentences 8-10.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that explains how the two rehearsal moments support the cellist's claim in sentence 4. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The contrast suggests that the players were timing their entrance to her breath.
options.label: correct
options.why: Links the together and ragged entrances to the claim that players follow her breath.

options.text: The overture was difficult, and the group rehearsed it many times that day.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Adds background and does not explain how the evidence supports the claim.

options.text: The cellist had played with the orchestra for several years before that.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Supports the cellist's credibility, not the link between evidence and claim.

options.text: This proves that a baton is useless and conductors should stop using one.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Overreaches far beyond what two entrances can show.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 10 so that it is concise and clearly shows that her gesture caused the same result each time. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: She lowered her hand, and the trumpets, which happened each time, softened.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The misplaced 'which' clause makes it unclear what happened each time.

options.text: She lowered her left hand slowly, although the trumpets softened each time.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: 'Although' signals contrast rather than cause.

options.text: Each time she slowly lowered her left hand, the trumpets softened.
options.label: correct
options.why: Concise; 'each time' plus the main clause clearly shows the repeated cause and effect.

options.text: Her left hand was lowered slowly, the trumpets got softer every single time.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Comma splice, and the passive voice is wordy.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 5 that gives further evidence for the cellist's specific claim in sentence 4, that the musicians follow the conductor's breath more closely than her baton. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Afterward, a violist told me she always keeps her eyes fixed on the tip of the conductor's baton.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Supports the baton instead of the breath, so it works against the claim.

options.text: Afterward, a violist told me that breathing exercises help wind players hold long notes more steadily.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Mentions breathing, but it's about players' own technique, not about following the conductor's breath.

options.text: Afterward, a violist told me she had been watching the conductor's rising shoulders, not the baton tip.
options.label: correct
options.why: A second player confirms she watched the breath (rising shoulders) rather than the baton, which directly supports the claim.

options.text: Afterward, a violist told me the overture is one of the hardest pieces the orchestra has learned.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Says how hard the piece is, which has nothing to do with breath or the baton.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a comparison after sentence 10 that advances her argument that a conductor's gestures are signals the players have learned to read. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Like a word in a shared language, the lowered hand meant softer only because the players had learned it together.
options.label: correct
options.why: The language comparison shows the gesture works through learned, shared meaning, which is the argument's main point.

options.text: Like a storm rolling slowly over the valley, the sound of the brass faded into the quiet hall.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: A decorative image of the sound fading that says nothing about how gestures carry meaning.

options.text: Like a painter at a blank canvas, she seemed to create the music entirely by herself.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Suggests she makes the music alone, which ignores the players reading her signals.

options.text: Like a traffic officer at a busy corner, she stood in the center where everyone could see her.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Compares her to someone who directs others, but the point is visibility, not learned signals.

items.stem: The writer's classmates have never been to an orchestra rehearsal. She wants to add a sentence after sentence 3 that tells these readers why a conductor's silence matters, so they see the puzzle her report looks into. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Yet forty teenagers with violins and horns somehow play as one group, so her silent signals must be telling them something.
options.label: correct
options.why: Uses a concrete picture a newcomer can follow and states the puzzle (how silence leads) that the report goes on to answer.

options.text: Musicologists have long debated whether ictus placement or preparatory gesture matters more in a conductor's technique.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Technical words like ictus and preparatory gesture will lose classmates who have never seen a rehearsal, and the sentence doesn't explain the puzzle.

options.text: Her baton is made of light wood with a cork handle, and she keeps it in a narrow case beside the podium.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: A physical detail that doesn't tell readers why her silence matters.

options.text: Everyone knows that conductors are the most important musicians in any orchestra anywhere in the world.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: A sweeping claim she can't back up, and it assumes knowledge these readers don't have.

items.stem: The writer wants to begin sentence 9 with a transition that shows the contrast between how often the conductor stopped the brass (sentence 8) and how calmly she did it. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Even so, the brass section was stopped often,
options.label: correct
options.why: 'Even so' sets her calm manner against how many times she interrupted, which is the contrast the writer wants.

options.text: As a result, the brass section was stopped often,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals cause and effect, but sentence 9 doesn't follow as a result of sentence 8.

options.text: For example, the brass section was stopped often,
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Calls sentence 9 an example, when it actually adds a contrast.

options.text: Similarly, the brass section was stopped often,
options.label: reversal
options.why: Signals similarity when the relationship is contrast.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace the underlined portion of sentence 9, "Honestly, the brass guys got kind of bossed around," with wording that fits the objective, academic tone a report for her music-history teacher calls for. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The brass players received frequent corrections,
options.label: correct
options.why: Neutral, exact and formal, and it still leads into the contrast with 'but she never raised her voice.'

options.text: The brass dudes totally got called out a bunch,
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Still slangy and casual.

options.text: The poor brass players were cruelly tormented,
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Dramatic and emotionally loaded, so it isn't objective, and it overstates what happened.

options.text: The brass players were somewhat corrected,
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Formal, but 'somewhat' is vague and loses the point that the corrections came often, which sentence 8 sets up.

blueprint.purpose: To show college admissions readers how working at a public pool shaped the writer's sense of civic responsibility
blueprint.claim: A public pool is a rare place where strangers become neighbors, and keeping such a place open takes people who will speak up for it.
blueprint.theme: public swimming pools as shared civic spaces

planned_flaws.flaw: Claim needs more specific evidence that strangers actually connect
Overstated claim that everyone agreed
Missing transition showing partial cause-effect
Slangy tone unsuited to admissions readers
Wordy, repetitive sentence
Conclusion drifts off purpose

g-lw44.title: Forty Lengths at Harrow Street
paragraphs: Every summer since I was fourteen, I have spent my mornings at the Harrow Street Pool in Calder Falls, first as a swimmer and now as a lifeguard.
Pools are important to communities in many ways.
At six in the morning, the lap lanes belong to retirees like Mr. Okafor, who swims exactly forty lengths and then tells me the water temperature as if I had not measured it myself.
By noon, the shallow end fills with day-camp kids whose counselors call out names in four languages.
The pool brings together people who would never otherwise meet.
Last July, I watched a retired machinist teach a nine-year-old girl from the apartments on Delmont Avenue how to float on her back, his hand flat beneath her spine until she no longer needed it.
Last spring, the city council proposed closing Harrow Street to save money.
Everyone in town agreed that this was a terrible idea.
I spoke at the budget hearing, holding a petition with 312 signatures I had collected at the snack bar.
The council kept the pool open, but it cut the evening hours, the only time many working parents could bring their children.
That decision was totally lame, and honestly it bugged me a lot.

What I learned from all of this is that the thing I learned is that a public space only stays public if the people who use it are willing to show up and speak up for it in the places where the decisions about it get made.
In conclusion, swimming is a very good form of exercise for people of all ages.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 13 with a conclusion that connects her experience at the pool to the kind of member she hopes to be in a college community. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Swimming at Harrow Street kept me healthy for years, and I plan to keep doing laps at whatever college pool I find next fall.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Focuses on exercise, not on civic engagement or community membership.

options.text: Public spaces of every kind, from parks to libraries to plazas, are the foundation of any healthy democratic society in the world.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Generalizes about society without connecting to the writer or college.

options.text: Wherever I go next, I want to be the one who knows the regulars by name and shows up at the meeting when their shared space is at risk.
options.label: correct
options.why: Links the pool lessons (knowing regulars, speaking up) to her future role in a new community.

options.text: Next summer I hope to earn my advanced lifeguard certification, which requires sixty hours of training and a timed rescue test.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Introduces a new, unrelated detail instead of concluding the essay's argument.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that provides further evidence for the claim in sentence 5 that the pool connects people who would otherwise never meet. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The girl practiced floating every afternoon after that, and by August she could swim the full width of the pool alone.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Follows the girl's progress but says nothing about a connection between people.

options.text: That summer the pool recorded more than nine thousand visits, its highest attendance since the snack bar was renovated.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Attendance shows popularity, not that strangers formed connections.

options.text: Most people agree that a cool pool is one of the most relaxing places to spend a hot afternoon in the middle of July.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: A vague generalization unrelated to people meeting.

options.text: Neither knew the other's name when the lesson began, and by August her mother was bringing him tomatoes from their balcony garden.
options.label: correct
options.why: Shows two strangers from different backgrounds forming an ongoing connection through the pool.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 11 so that it conveys her frustration in a tone appropriate for college admissions readers. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The decision frustrated me, because the families who most needed the pool had lost the only hours they could use it.
options.label: correct
options.why: Expresses frustration in measured, mature language and gives a reason.

options.text: That decision represented an unconscionable betrayal of every citizen, a wound upon the very soul of Calder Falls.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Melodramatic and inflated rather than sincere.

options.text: The decision was a total disaster, and it made me so mad that I could barely stand to look at the council members.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Remains overly emotional and informal for admissions readers.

options.text: The decision reduced operational hours by approximately three per day, effective at the start of the fiscal year.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Clinical and detached; drops the frustration entirely.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 2 so that it gives college admissions readers, who look for personal reflection, a clear sense of what the pool came to mean to her. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Honestly, the pool is basically the best spot in Calder Falls, and everybody knows it.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Uses casual, boastful phrasing and an unsupported claim instead of thoughtful reflection.

options.text: Lifeguards must be certified in first aid and must renew that certification every two years.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Gives a procedural fact that has nothing to do with the essay's reflective claim.

options.text: Public pools across the country offer recreation, safety training, and relief from summer heat.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Makes a general statement about pools nationwide and leaves out the writer's own reflection.

options.text: Over those summers, I came to see the pool as one of the few places in town where strangers become neighbors.
options.label: correct
options.why: Offers a personal insight drawn from her experience and previews the essay's claim, which is what admissions readers look for.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 that explains how the council's decision weakens the role she says the pool plays in the community. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The council also discussed repaving Delmont Avenue and repainting the library that night.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Moves to unrelated agenda items rather than commenting on the pool decision.

options.text: Even so, the pool stayed open, so the petition clearly achieved everything it set out to do.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Says the outcome was a full success, which goes against the writer's point that the cut did real harm.

options.text: Without those hours, the families who most needed a shared place to meet their neighbors were the ones left out.
options.label: correct
options.why: Links the lost evening hours to the claim that the pool brings strangers together, showing who is now cut off.

options.text: The evening lifeguards were reassigned to the morning shift, which was already fully staffed.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Adds a staffing detail that has no basis in the draft and does not explain the effect on the community.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 12 so that it is concise and states her lesson without repetition. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: I learned that public spaces matter to everyone in many different ways.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Concise, but it loses the specific point about showing up where decisions are made.

options.text: I learned that a public space stays public, so its users show up wherever decisions are made.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: "So" reverses the condition and makes it sound as if staying public causes people to show up.

options.text: What I learned is that the lesson I learned is that public spaces need people to speak up for them.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Shortens the sentence but keeps the redundant "learned" construction.

options.text: I learned that a public space stays public only if its users show up and speak up where decisions are made.
options.label: correct
options.why: Removes the repeated "I learned" and the wordy phrasing but keeps the full lesson.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence at the end of paragraph 1 that states a thesis needing proof and previews both halves of the essay: the pool bringing people together and the fight to keep it open. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Those mornings started at six o'clock, and I have worked at the pool for several summers, first swimming and later guarding.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It repeats facts from sentence 1 and makes no claim, so it cannot serve as a thesis.

options.text: Those mornings taught me that every public space in every town shapes the character of the citizens who happen to use it.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: It is too sweeping for what one essay can prove, and it previews neither the pool's specific role nor the hearing.

options.text: Those mornings taught me that a pool can turn strangers into neighbors, and that it stays open only if someone will stand up for it.
options.label: correct
options.why: It makes an arguable claim and points ahead to paragraph 2 (strangers connecting) and paragraph 3 (speaking at the hearing).

options.text: Those mornings taught me that a pool can turn strangers into neighbors, from retirees in the lap lanes to campers in the shallow end.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: It previews only the community half and leaves out the civic fight in paragraph 3.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 6 so that it begins with a phrase describing the machinist standing in the water, and the phrase must clearly and correctly modify him. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Standing waist-deep beside her last July, I watched a retired machinist teach a nine-year-old girl from Delmont Avenue to float.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The phrase now attaches to the narrator, not to the machinist the writer meant to describe.

options.text: Standing waist-deep beside her last July; a retired machinist taught a nine-year-old girl from Delmont Avenue to float on her back.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The modifier is in the right place, but the semicolon wrongly cuts the phrase off from the main clause.

options.text: Standing waist-deep beside her last July, a nine-year-old girl from Delmont Avenue was taught to float by a retired machinist.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: This is a misplaced modifier: the phrase seems to describe the girl, not the machinist.

options.text: Standing waist-deep beside her last July, a retired machinist taught a nine-year-old girl from Delmont Avenue to float on her back.
options.label: correct
options.why: The opening phrase sits right next to the noun it describes, the machinist, so the modifier is placed correctly.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 8 so that it admits some residents saw things differently while still showing that she, and many others, opposed the closure. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Some residents thought the savings were worth it, but many families who swam there saw the closure as a real loss.
options.label: correct
options.why: It replaces the overstated 'everyone' with a fair opposing view and keeps the writer's position, which sets up her speaking at the hearing in sentence 9.

options.text: A few people backed the plan, though they were plainly wrong and had probably never even swum there.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: It mentions the other side only to mock it, which undercuts the fair-minded civic voice admissions readers expect.

options.text: Nearly everyone in Calder Falls agreed that this was a terrible and shortsighted idea.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: 'Nearly' softens the claim a little, but it still leaves out any opposing view.

options.text: Most residents backed the plan, since the pool cost the city far more than it could afford.
options.label: reversal
options.why: It drops the writer's opposition and states an unsupported claim about cost, which makes her petition seem out of place.

items.stem: In sentence 3, the writer wants to replace the portion after 'forty lengths and' with wording that shows fond amusement toward Mr. Okafor, not irritation, in a tone suited to admissions readers. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: then reports the water temperature to me, a daily ritual I have come to look forward to
options.label: correct
options.why: The wording is warm and gently humorous, and it suits the essay's point that the pool builds bonds between people.

options.text: then annoyingly informs me of a water temperature I have obviously already measured
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Words like 'annoyingly' and 'obviously' turn the line into irritation, the opposite of fondness.

options.text: then states the water temperature, which is also recorded hourly on the deck chart
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It is neutral and only gives information, so the affection the writer wants is gone.

options.text: then tells me the temperature, which is kind of hilarious since checking it is basically my job
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: 'Kind of hilarious' and 'basically' are too casual for an admissions essay.
